note: Tap a bowl of water on the rim and the ripples run inward; touch the center and they run outward. Thomas's voice came from the ring to Dante at the center, and Beatrice's now goes from the center back to the ring.

context: He has just finished his lesson on Solomon's wisdom, and does not speak again in the poem.
She asks on Dante's behalf a question he has not yet even formed.

note: The souls here appear only as blazing lights. Beatrice asks two things: will that brightness last forever, and if so, how will their eyes stand it once they have bodies again?
At the Last Judgment. Christians believe that at the end of time the dead will rise and every soul will be joined again to its own body. This resurrection of the flesh is the subject of the answer.
The grace and joy that God pours down on the blessed without end.

quote: The One and Two and Three
context: A hymn to God as one in nature and three in Persons. The "Two" is usually taken as the two natures of Christ, divine and human.

note: Nothing bounds or contains God, and God contains everything.

context: The speaker is not named, but Thomas called Solomon the most beautiful light of the inner ring in Canto 10. He may be chosen to speak of the body because the Song of Songs, a poem of bodily love, was held to be his.
The angel Gabriel came to her to announce that she would bear the Son of God (Luke 1). A voice that tells of the glorified body recalls the one that told of God taking a body.

note: A chain of causes. Grace gives each soul its power to see God. From seeing comes love, and from love comes the light that shines around it. Sight comes first and love follows: this is the teaching of Thomas Aquinas.
The vision of God is always a gift. It is greater than anything the soul's own merits could earn.
The risen body will not be the old frail one. Theologians taught that it will be glorified: bright, free of pain and unable to die.
A human being is soul and body together, and a soul without its body is only part of a person. So the blessed will be more perfect after the resurrection, not less, and will see and love God more.
Freely given light. Theologians called it the light of glory: a gift that strengthens the mind so that it can look on God, which no creature can do by its own power.
A coal in the fire glows so white that it can be seen through the flame wrapped around it. In the same way the risen body will show through the soul's light, and outshine it.
The bodies of the blessed lie in their graves until the Last Judgment.
One of the most human moments in the Paradiso. The blessed lack nothing, yet they long for their bodies, and for the day when they will see again the faces of those they loved on earth.
A third ring of souls begins to appear around the other two. Dante never says who they are. With the cry to the Holy Spirit that follows, the three circles are often read as an image of the Trinity.
The light of the souls is the glow of their love, and love is the special name of the Holy Spirit, the third Person of the Trinity.
As always in Paradise, the ascent takes no time. Dante only knows he has risen because what he sees has changed.

context: Dante and Beatrice arrive. The planet seems to redden further, as if smiling in welcome.

note: The wordless speech of the heart, which is the same in every people.
Dante's word is olocausto, a burnt offering: the whole of himself given up in thanks. It suits the heaven of those who gave their lives.
Two broad bands of light crossing each other, each made of countless souls.
Dante's Italian has Eliòs, from Helios, the Greek word for the sun, with an echo of the Hebrew name for God, Eli. It is God who is addressed, the sun that lights these souls.
The Milky Way. Ancient and medieval thinkers disagreed about what it was; Dante reviews their theories in his Convivio and leans to the view that it is a mass of stars too small to see one by one.
Draw two diameters at right angles in a circle and it is divided into four quadrants. The lines form a cross with four equal arms, and that is the shape here.
In Dante's Italian these three rhyming lines all end in Cristo. Dante never rhymes the name with any word but itself. What he saw, whether a figure or only a flash, he says he cannot describe.
Christ's words: "If anyone would come after me, let him deny himself and take up his cross and follow me" (Matthew 16). The souls here did so to the death.
The souls of those who fought for the faith. Several are named in Canto 18, among them Joshua, Charlemagne and Roland.
Dust motes drifting in a beam of sunlight that slants into a shuttered room. The shade people "contrive" is the house, with its blinds, built to keep out the sun.
The only words Dante catches of the hymn. They are addressed to Christ, risen from the dead and victorious over death.
Beatrice's. He has just said that nothing had ever held him like this song, which seems to rank it above her.
Usually taken to be the heavens, which stamp their influence on the world below and grow more beautiful the higher one climbs. Some read the phrase as Beatrice's eyes themselves.

The joy of Beatrice's eyes. Dante's Italian is hard, and is usually read to mean that her beauty is not being set aside by his praise of the song: it too grows purer with each heaven, and he has not yet looked at her in this one.
